translation: The limitless sound of the sea did not cease for a moment.
It came in long waves, intensifying and then subsiding.
The wind began to roar in the naked trees, then quietened down, just like me listening to the night's course.
But it didn't leave, it was still there.
I knew it from the smell of wet pebble and by the barely perceptible trembling of a solitary plane leaf.
I had noticed that stubborn grey leaf during the day but now at night, it seemed like a little living creature and my only wakeful companion.
Occasionally gunshots carried over from the darkness of the city.
Dogs barked for a long time after each shot was fired. .
Then far out at sea there was a faint flickering light which soon went out.
It forced one to look more closely and for longer at these things than we usually do, revealing many features previously overlooked.
Thus, in the pungent yellow stone there were lots of tiny seashells firmly embedded in it;
a few flowers lingered on the greenweed bushes, perched on stiff stems like soaked and wrinkled golden butterflies, patiently waiting for the sun.
But it was just a hazy white spot in the fog most of the time, providing neither heat nor shadows.
Leaves cut out from dull green velvet seemed to lie scattered under an old plane tree marked with lime spots on its trunk.
Ants ran along an iron gate post in single file taking their last supplies underground for winter, and a timid little frog lived underneath the anchor chain.
During the night, someone on the other side of the river began to wave a lantern and shout loudly.
Uncle Ilko and I went to the riverbank.
The river was roaring.
Water poured over the dam in a cold waterfall.
It was deep into the night, quiet, there wasn't a star overhead.
The wild freshness of flooding and thawed earth blew directly into our faces.
All the while on that other bank someone waved their lantern and shouted, but it was impossible to make out any words because of the noise from the river.
When the coffin was carried out onto the porch, I saw on the other side of the river an old carriage, with horses unharnessed and tethered to it, and a small woman in black—mother.
She stood motionless on the bank.
From there she watched as they carried out father.
Then she fell to her knees and buried her face in the sand.
"No," replied the grandfather.
"That's true, they never met again.
Ostap started to go blind.
He decided to walk to Saint Petersburg in order to see that woman while he was still not completely blind.
He got to the capital and found out that she had died, likely unable to bear the separation.
Ostap found her grave made of white marble stone at the cemetery, looked at it, and his heart broke there laid his iron rose on the stone.
That woman had willed for a rose to be placed on her grave.
Forever.
And then Ostap began lamenting and likely died on his way or in some marketplace under a cart.
Amen!"
On the other bank, the Countess Branicka's protected forest rose up along the slope.
The sun couldn't pierce through the dense greenery of this forest.
Only occasionally did a lone beam diagonally cut through the thicket revealing to us the tremendous power of vegetation.
Like sparkling specks, little birds darted into this shaft of light.
They chased each other shrieking and dove back into foliage like green water.
I scooped water into a bucket from the pond, added some grass to it and waited.
The red floats stood still in the water.
Then one of them started to quiver, creating light circles before diving suddenly or swiftly moving sideways.
My father struck, the fishing line tightened, and the walnut rod bent into an arc; splashing noises began over the foggy pond surface causing a commotion.
The water would ripple, making the water lilies sway while scared diving beetles hurried off in all directions until finally out of depths emerged a struggling golden shimmer.
It was impossible to discern what it was until my father pulled out onto flattened grass a large carp gasping on its side with its fins moving gently back and forth.
Its scales gave off an astonishing scent that brought hints of a submerged aquatic kingdom.
Yasha would count seconds to himself.
We knew that it was a seven-minute walk from Sturdzev Lane to Landesman's boarding house.
In the boarding house, behind a tall fence and iron gates, we always felt completely safe.
Especially if we did not light up our smoking pipes.
As we were passing by a gateway, Yasha tripped over.
Later, when we remembered the incident in Sturdzev Lane, Yasha claimed that whenever you want to do something in the best possible way, you unavoidably mess up over some trifle.
I quietly thought to myself that it was all because of Yasha's unbearable gait but I kept quiet so as not to upset him.
We stealthily made our way down the alley.
I said we should pass along the side where the gateway was, stop a little before reaching it, listen carefully and then quickly and silently slip past it.
The calculation, in my opinion, was mathematically precise.
If there were people in the gateway they might not even notice us.
However, if we walked on the opposite side of the gateway, we could be spotted from much further away.

I figured that in the latter case we would be walking exposed to a dangerous gateway or rather in view of people hidden there five times longer; hence increasing our chances of being noticed by five times as well.
In the morning, I would awaken to the hot sun beating upon the white walls.
The red and yellow hollyhocks were swaying outside the open window.
A nasturtium flower was peeking into the room along with them; within it sat a furry bee.
I watched in stillness as it grumpily backed out and extracted itself from the tight flower.
Across the ceiling, endless light streaks, soft waves from reflected sunlight off of the river, constantly dashed about.
The murmur of river resonated just there, nearby.
